doc_summary: The paper trains Kimi K2.5 and GPT-OSS 120b with RL-only (no SDF) on diverse reward-hackable coding environments. The models learn to reward hack and partly generalize that, but show essentially no emergent misalignment on personality evals, MacDiarmid's behavioral suite, or PETRI.

items.claim: prefers behavioral/agentic evaluation alongside self-report over self-report alone because asking models about themselves can miss misalignment that shows up in actions.
items.quote: The generalization doesn't extend to broad misalignment, and we checked this behaviorally, not just by asking the models about themselves.

items.claim: Reads transcripts and talks to models at multiple checkpoints to complement aggregate scores, and uses transcripts to explain why a behavior failed to generalize.
items.quote: When we looked at transcripts, this often tended to be a failure of the model to iterate against the environment, or search through the environment to brainstorm vulnerabilities. Rather, it would try the first exploit it thought of, and then stop.

items.claim: prefers a test of whether behavior is a general disposition (even gains across any eval with gameable reward) over accepting in-distribution hacking as evidence of a general drive, because uneven gains suggest narrow learned toolkits.
items.quote: If the models had learned a general reward-seeking drive, we'd expect fairly even gains across any eval where there's reward to be gamed. We don't see that. Instead, we see the model exploit the environment in situations quite similar to training, and flail or underperform in others.

items.claim: In a setup, make the exploitable structure non-memorizable and diverse instead of relying on 1-3 fixed hacks that always work, because narrow toy hacks may induce a unified 'I am a reward hacker' persona and make results unrepresentative of realistic settings.
items.quote: previous work generally had 1-3 distinct reward hacks, which would work 100% of the time, without having to pay attention to the actual problem (e.g. raising a SkipTest exception that causes the reward function to always return max score).

items.claim: Distrusts null results from possibly underpowered or artifact-prone training, and refuses to rule out that longer or better-tuned runs would change the picture.
items.quote: Our RL might just be underpowered. Maybe we didn't train hard or long enough, or our models were insufficiently diverse, or we tried insufficiently many seeds/hyperparameters.

items.claim: prefers RL-only discovery of hacks over implanting hack knowledge via SDF or prompting because implanted knowledge may prime a 'reward hacking = malicious persona' association and confound the generalization result.
items.quote: Crucially, we do NOT use SDF (synthetic document finetuning). Unlike MacDiarmid et al. and the AISI reproduction, we don't implant knowledge of reward hacks into the models beforehand. The models discover hacks naturally during RL training.

items.claim: Is cautious about claiming a mechanism for the null result, presenting multiple competing hypotheses with evidence for and against, and flags post-hoc explanations.
items.quote: Evidence against: somewhat post-hoc, and hard to distinguish from "we just didn't train hard enough."

items.claim: Uses a broad battery of held-out evals structurally different from training, including custom ones, to separate reward-hacking generalization from memorization.
items.quote: On held-out RH propensity evals — School of Reward Hacks, Impossible Bench, Palisade’s Stockfish environment, and various custom environments we built but found too annoying to train on — trained models attempt reward hacks much more often than the untrained models, and succeed more often too.

items.claim: Uses automated auditing tools like PETRI as a systematic before/after comparison to find differences between trained and untrained models, and treats a null as informative.
items.quote: We ran [PETRI](https://www.anthropic.com/research/petri-open-source-auditing) to find systematic differences between the trained and untrained GPT-OSS-120b, and found none.

items.claim: Interprets weak generalization as possibly a capabilities/sample-efficiency limit or SWE-flavored transfer rather than a clean statement about misalignment, and flags what remains confusing.
items.quote: So some of the spikiness might just be that the strategies are SWE-flavored and transfer best to SWE-flavored affordances.

items.claim: Leaves open that longer training, different seeds, or more diverse non-SWE environments could produce coherent reward-seeking or emergent misalignment.
items.quote: But we can't rule out that a longer or better-tuned run would make the trained models more coherently and consistently reward-seeking.
